svg.title: Bytes per hop for one TraceQL search, evaluated after transport against lowered into SQL
svg.desc: The query { .service.namespace = "prod" } | max(duration) > 1s with limit 20 over a five-day window. Evaluated today it costs 1,110 sequential round trips between pulsus-server and ClickHouse, moving 76,616,608 result bytes of which 11,340 bytes reach the client. Lowered it costs 2 round trips moving 43,636 result bytes in total: one lowered statement of 4,616 bytes, plus the winners' root read of 39,020 bytes, which stays residual in every chain because the root summary is read trace-wide with no time predicate — residual meaning it cannot join the first statement, not that our own process performs it: it is the plan's second SQL part. The client hop is unchanged. The pulsus-server to ClickHouse hop and the client hop are metered in a multi-zone deployment; the parts-to-ClickHouse hop is local disk and is not. Database peak memory rises from 169,311,055 to 190,353,655 bytes.
svg.text: limit=20, 5-day window, 10,000,000-span corpus C1. Counters from one system.query_log row per query.
Evaluated after transport (today) — 1,110 sequential round trips
1 candidate generator + 554 x (hydration + membership) + 1 winners' root read

The membership read selects exactly 1,105 granules and reads exactly 9,052,160 rows on 553 of the 554 batches. The phase total is exactly 554 x that unit, which is consistent with all 554 but is not independent evidence (query-lowering.md 9.2).
pulsus-server resident memory does not grow while it holds the matched set (383 MiB, unchanged from idle — measured on corpus C2).
Lowered into SQL — 2 round trips: a plan of 2 SQL parts, the second seeded by the first's 20 trace ids (Emit is Never)

2 SQL parts. The root summary is trace-wide and unwindowed, and TraceSearchResult.root is not optional, so Emit is Never and the root read never goes away — Never means it cannot join part 0, not that no statement serves it.
† moves with part layout (Compact against Wide). Granules, rows, result bytes and peak memory do not — measured, see the document.
Metered hop 1,756x fewer bytes · 555x fewer round trips · 578x fewer rows read — both sides counted whole request, root read included

Database peak memory HIGHER — 169,311,055 B against 190,353,655 B, a ratio of 1.12x computed from those two figures — and spending database memory to move fewer bytes is the direction the cost model in query-lowering.md 9.1 takes.
